Matthias
muh-THY-uhs
proper noun (person)
Greek Maththias, from Hebrew Mattithyah, "gift of YHWH"; the disciple chosen by lot to replace Judas among the twelve apostles.

See also: Matthias

Biblical Definition

Matthias was the disciple chosen to take the place of Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles, restoring their number before Pentecost. In the days between the ascension and Pentecost, Peter stood among the gathered believers and explained from the Psalms that another must take the office Judas had forfeited (Acts 1:20). The qualification was specific: he must be one "which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us... a witness with us of his resurrection" (Acts 1:21-22). Two men met the standard: Joseph called Barsabbas, and Matthias. The believers prayed, asking the Lord who knows all hearts to show His choice, and cast lots; "and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles" (Acts 1:26). Of his later labors Scripture says nothing further; tradition holds he preached and was martyred. Matthias stands in the dictionary as the apostle chosen to complete the Twelve, a witness of the resurrection from the beginning, whose selection by prayer and lot shows the early church seeking the mind of the Lord, and whose quiet entrance into the apostolic college testifies that God knows and appoints His servants, even those Scripture names but once.

Webster 1828 Definition

The disciple chosen by lot (Acts 1:23-26) to replace Judas among the twelve apostles; a witness of Christ's resurrection from John's baptism onward, selected after the believers prayed for the Lord to show His choice.

MATTHIAS, proper noun. "Gift of YHWH"; chosen to replace Judas among the twelve apostles.

Selected in the days between the ascension and Pentecost (Acts 1:15-26).

Qualified as a witness of Christ from John's baptism to the ascension.

One of two candidates, with Joseph Barsabbas.

Chosen by lot after prayer; "numbered with the eleven apostles."

Key Scripture

Acts 1:21 — "Wherefore of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,"

Acts 1:22 — "Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection."

Acts 1:24 — "And they prayed, and said, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen,"

Acts 1:26 — "And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles."

Modern Corruption

Matthias's choosing honors the recovery of the apostolic qualification — eyewitness of the risen Christ — and of the church seeking God's choice in prayer, against a casual view of office and a doubt that questions God's ordering of His church.

expand to see more

Office-trivialized correction. The apostleship was no honorary title but a specific office requiring eyewitness testimony to the risen Christ. Matthias qualified because he had companied with the Lord from the beginning and seen Him risen. The dictionary holds that the foundational apostolic witness was grounded in eyewitness fact, not later invention; the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph 2:20), men who had seen the Lord and could testify of His resurrection.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is seeking the Lord's choice in prayer. The believers did not lobby or campaign but prayed, "Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen" (Acts 1:24). The dictionary commends their dependence: in the choosing of leaders the church is to seek the mind of the Lord who knows all hearts, trusting Him to appoint His own servants, as He appointed Matthias to complete the Twelve.
